utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Just before you commence, Ms. Somers, I would just draw attention to two decisions of the Chamber which were filed last evening, copies of which I believe have been distributed to counsel this morning, concerning the 92 bis application and the Defence objections to the Prosecution's opening statement. Now, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, and thank you very much, Your Honours. I would like to call the Chamber's attention to the fact that I'm informed that our Sanction function is not operative at this moment. So there may be some difficulties in the visual presentation with respect to a video. We will see if there's any improvement during the course of the sessions. If not, then we would attempt to use an original, and then request the Chamber's leave to put in an appropriate copy, of course, providing to the Defence as well. Otherwise, there is -- there are physical copies of things available. We regret this. I think the change of courtrooms and the updating of a system last weekend, updating in inverted commas, has caused us a little grief, and I apologise for any inconvenience to the Chamber. The Prosecution is still in the course of examining in chief Mr. Nikola Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If Mr. Samardzic could be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Samardzic, and good morning to you. If I could remind you that you are still subject to the affirmation you gave at the commencement of your evidence. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When we left off, just to take you back - it's been a few days - we were discussing, and you had just indicated in response to my question the distance between Trebinje and Dubrovnik, and you had indicated 24 kilometres. There had been a discussion before that about a person named Vucurevic, and I would like to ask you if you could explain something you said in response to my question. I had asked: "Are you aware of any particular attitude that Mr. Vucurevic held toward Dubrovnik, and particularly during the time of this conflict?" Part of your response, a part of your response, was: "He said he was the tourism person and would run tourism the way he saw fit and when he saw fit." I wonder, please: Are you able to explain what you understood the meaning of this to be, the relationship of Mr. Vucurevic to tourism, and how he could run it as he saw fit, when he saw fit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in fact quite a savage threat, that Dubrovnik would be demolished. He knew that Dubrovnik was a tourist centre in the southern part of the Adriatic Coast, and now that Dubrovnik was attacked and being demolished, his intention was to create a new form of tourism. It was well known that he had said: "I'm going to build a new old Dubrovnik," meaning that he was going to destroy the old one and build a new one. So he had made these kind of jokes and jests in order to demean Dubrovnik and turn it into something that was supposed to be the subject of ridicule. So these are kind of peasant jokes that maybe common people saw as humorous. However, this kind of humour was built on crime, on the destruction of a town, and even deaths of people. So if you target hotels, there's a risk of killing people there. And therefore, Vucurevic is greatly responsible for the events that had taken place in and around Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any name or title he may have used about himself in relation to Dubrovnik and tourism?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to call himself the minister of tourism of Dubrovnik, so that was another of his jokes. That was actually partly true, because through his activities, he brought a lot of evil and bad things for the tourism of Dubrovnik, because there were not too many tourists coming at the time there. His title was the president of the town of Trebinje, while he was just a common truck driver. However, he gained popularity in Trebinje and its environs due to his ultranationalist attitudes and his hatred towards the Croats and the Muslims. This has elevated him to a position that he had held, that is, the mayor, and he became influential among the people advocating the aggression on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Mr. Samardzic, with a formation, a military formation, entitled "the Trebinje Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never saw this brigade, but I did hear about it very much in Boka Kotorska, that this brigade did exist and took part in the battles around Dubrovnik. It was well known that it took part in the looting and demolishing. It was composed of people from Herzegovina, not only from Trebinje but from other places, like Bileca and other places. Everyone they managed to mobilise joined this brigade, and this brigade was very, very active.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you know, if you know, are you able to tell us where the headquarters of the 2nd Operational Group that you referred to with respect to the Dubrovnik conflict, if you know where the headquarters were, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly where the headquarters was situated during the Dubrovnik operation, because, as far as I know, it changed places. At one time it was in Trebinje, and then was relocated around the theatre of battle, as was requested. So I couldn't know exactly where the command of the 2nd Operational Group was. But as I said last time, I had means of getting in touch, through Pavle Bulatovic, the minister of foreign affairs. However, the exact location was never disclosed. I heard that it was Trebinje and some other places near Dubrovnik, such as Kumbor and other places. But I cannot say surely, because nobody had ever told me exactly the location, because I was not part of the military, so they didn't tell me where the command of the 2nd Operational Group was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You mentioned Pavle Bulatovic, and it said minister of foreign affairs. Is that what you meant, Pavle Bulatovic was minister of ...

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a slip of the tongue. Pavle Bulatovic was the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Pavle Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samardzic. Mr. Samardzic, just for a point of clarification: You referred to the term "Herzegovina." Would you be able, very briefly, to describe what area you are referring to when you say "Herzegovina," in connection with the comment about the headquarters of the 2nd Operational Group? What is Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Herzegovina is part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In fact, that is the south-western part of the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It stretches between the River Neretva, up to the Montenegrin border. That is the width of this area. And from the south to the north, it ran along the Croatian border, which means very close to Dubrovnik, up to the River Sutjeska and the place called Cemar. Now, this is the area that is commonly referred to as Herzegovina, and the places there are Gacko, Bileca, Trebinje, Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not Trebinje was included in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Trebinje is in Herzegovina, and this is the second largest town in Herzegovina after Mostar. However, we should add that part of Montenegro used to be part of Herzegovina. However, after the liberation from the Turkish occupation in 1878, this part of Herzegovina became part of Montenegro. So this particular area is now in Montenegro, located to the east from Trebinje and Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, as you were minister of foreign affairs on the 8th of October, 1991, I wanted to take a very brief couple of moments to ask you, by recalling a document which is already in evidence - we have copies for the Chamber. It is from P20, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are sufficient copies for counsel as well. I believe we'll have to use the ELMO because of Sanction. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, if you could take a look at the document in front of you. It is labelled -- it is from the Assembly of the Republic of Montenegro of Titograd, October 8, 1991, and it is signed by a person, or purports to be signed by a person named Dr. Risto Vukcevic. Do you know such a person?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Risto Vukcevic was the president of the parliament of Montenegro. Unfortunately, he died. But at the time, he was the speaker of the Montenegrin parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you know of his functions during the course -- on the 8th of October, 1991? Are you aware of his relationship to this document? Did you have any particular role to play in either the drafting or implementation of this document, called "Initiative"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his capacity of the president of the Montenegrin parliament, he signed this document, but it was me who drafted the document. These were attempts, in that difficult situation when the war had already broken out, to find a solution in order to put an end to the war. And we appealed to the president of the Croatian parliament, Mr. Domljan, to start negotiations, claiming that we in Montenegro played no parts in the aggression on Croatia, although we did, in fact, have, because our boys were very much engaged and involved in the army. But we, as the government, wanted to distance ourselves on the 7th October 1991 from the whole affair and to initiate a procedure in order to bring peace. In that sense, I wrote this initiative, which was accepted by both Miro and Momir, and signed by Risto Vukcevic. I established direct telephone line with the Croats, because other telephone lines were severed. I had to buy a special telephone in Italy and to have a beacon on a hill, so via Italy, I was able to converse with Zagreb. That was how we established this communication. And it resulted in many people from the counter-intelligence service being surprised, because they knew that we were communicating with someone, but they couldn't find out in what way. This was no intelligence or spy operation. We were simply trying to establish contacts with Croatia in order to conduct at least some kind of negotiations with them. After that, an initiative was launched, and the response came from Croatia, which was favourable. We were invited to come to Zagreb to see Mr. Domljan and to have these negotiations with him. However, at the last minute, Momir Bulatovic stopped this initiative and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, can I just ask you to help us possibly correct something in the record. On page 7, line 9, you said: "I wrote this initiative, which was accepted by both --" and the record says Miro, M-i-r-o, and Momir. Did you mean Miro, M-i-r-o, or another name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted this document and took it to them to show it to them. They made no objections to it, and they basically saw it as something that is -- that doesn't have too many prospects for success. Therefore, they were not either against this, but they were not also very enthusiastic about it, because the war was going on. Risto and I, however, counted that something would come out of that, and the only correction that I see here, on page 2 in the statement of reasons, when I explained in my letter that Montenegro would not allow or would not be good to allow to establish a military base in Boka Kotorska, even if that was the friendly army of Croatia. My version was a brotherly army from Croatia. That was the only change, because I was warned that we cannot be brothers because we were at war. Otherwise, everything remained as it is, and this version was sent to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify again: When you say "Miro and Momir," whom do you refer to? Could we have their correct, full names.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat: Momir Bulatovic, he was the first one to whom I took the document, and I showed it to Milo Djukanovic, who was the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was -- I just wanted to make sure that we understood each other. Just a couple of questions about this document. Paragraph 1, I will refer to the English, if you're comfortable, at least for purposes of this document. Taking into consideration the decision -- excuse me. I'll back up. Initiative for the determination of the sea and land border between the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia, by agreement. Now, the subject matter of this document, then, is -- relates to borders or issues that concern borders; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And it is a direct communication from Montenegro to Croatia, is that correct, without Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's fine to answer in your native language, sir. I just wanted to have you read it, if you didn't mind.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the initiative shows, in my opinion, the launching of this initiative, shows determination on the part of the Republic of Croatia to become an independent state. The Assembly of Montenegro decided that, in addition to opening up a number of state issues between the two states, would also entail the changing of present-day borders between Croatia and Montenegro. It is by saying this that the parliament of Montenegro recognises the independence of the Republic of Croatia, which up to that point, no one had recognised, with the possible exception of Slovenia. The Montenegrin parliament states clearly: We hereby recognise the independence of the Republic of Croatia and its sovereignty. This is a contradiction. We are at war. We are fighting each other, yet the parliament says that we recognise Croatia's independence. In addition to this statement, also the issue of the sea border is being raised, which was necessary at the time. There had been one state, and now there was secession, separation. Therefore, both sea and land borders had to be determined. The land border existed, the old administrative border, where the Prevlaka area belonged to Croatia, but the sea border remained to be determined, because there had been no border up to that point between Croatia and Montenegro. The sea was shared. What this initiative makes clear is that Croatia and Montenegro must start negotiations to determine the exact border of the internal waters in the Boka Kotorska Bay and in the Epi continental belt surrounding Boka Kotorska Bay at the open sea. I think this was in full compliance with international law, and Croatia did indeed agree to negotiate with us on these issues. This, however, was abruptly interrupted, probably pursuant to orders from Belgrade, just several days later, and we could not follow up with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, was it contemplated, or does this document that you participated in drafting contemplate direct, continued contact between Montenegro and Croatia over matters such as borders?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document clearly shows that we had direct contact with Croatia in order to resolve these issues. These issues have not been fully resolved to this very day, ten years later. The sea border has still not been determined in the Boka Bay, between Croatia and Montenegro. There has been a great success, though, because it was officially recognised that the Prevlaka area belonged to Croatia. As for the sea border, it still remains to be determined by a special commission. Back then, when this document was written, to say that Prevlaka belonged to Croatia was a mark of treason for most of the printed media in Boka and in Montenegro. Whoever said that Prevlaka belonged to Croatia was either considered as mad or as a traitor. I remember my own experience. There was a journalist who wrote that I was totally out of my mind if I was saying that Prevlaka was Croatian, to begin with, and then I wanted to negotiate. My intention was to get Prevlaka, the area, by negotiations, peacefully. I did not want to conquer it by waging war on the Croats. I wanted to negotiate over Prevlaka, and this for many people meant that I was mad, that I was not in my right state of mind. Because their strategy was that they should have something that wasn't theirs. It's been quite long since, and in the meantime, all these clever people have finally ended up recognising that Prevlaka belonged to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, the very last paragraph of the initiative, above the sign-off, as it were, by Dr. Vukcevic, establishes a contact person for the Croatian parliament to work through on behalf of the Montenegrin side. And who is established as that contact person for continued contacts over territorial issues and other issues that are dealt with in this document? It is at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This last paragraph, or item 4, it says that negotiations should continue, that we should continue negotiations with Croatia, and I was appointed as the person who should run these negotiations. There was also Asim Dizdarevic, in addition to myself. He was the vice-president of the Montenegrin Assembly. And another person whom I cannot remember at the moment. On the Croatian side, there were Hrvoje Kacic, Zarko Domljan. When I look more closely at this document, because I have forgotten all about it in the meantime, they expected us to come to Zagreb first, and that was the original agreement. On the 25th of October, we were supposed to show up in Zagreb and start negotiations on Prevlaka and other issues that remained to be resolved. But then we couldn't go, and that's what was eventually said. In this difficult situation, when Dubrovnik was being fired on and demolished, we wanted to have negotiations, but getting Prevlaka was not our sole aim. We wanted to put an end to the war. However, we were in no position to order General Strugar to stop fighting and to stop the war. We were looking for ways to have negotiations that would eventually force the army to cease hostilities. The whole initiative was about this, re-establishing peace, although the very first thing that was said during those negotiations were all about Prevlaka. We were all perfectly aware that Prevlaka was not the crux of the matter, although it seemed foremost in the media and in people's stories. We knew that the most important thing was that Dubrovnik was being demolished, and this had to be stopped. Everyone did whatever they could. Some did more and some did less to stop this. However, Montenegro's leadership, especially those of us who tried to do something about it, and I was not the only one, were facing a very delicate situation. We were out to achieve something at a time when weapons were firing. And as we say in Montenegro, when heads are falling, it's difficult to achieve anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, was this initiative, to your knowledge, communicated to the Croatian parliament? Did they in fact acknowledge receipt of it? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know receipt and answer, and I have this on me right now as we speak. They received everything. They were glad to receive that. Their answer was very favourable, and they agreed to talk to us, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, just to clarify, and I don't have a map up now, but perhaps if you could give us a description of where Prevlaka is located, just points of orientation, if it's not too difficult to do verbally.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shouldn't be too difficult. Prevlaka is a narrow strip of land, a narrow strip, which is at the mouth of the Boka Bay. It's long, but it's small, so you can reach the open sea from inside the bay. That's precisely why it's called Prevlaka, an isthmus. It's several kilometres long and closes off, in a manner of speaking, the Boka Bay. This belongs to the Konavle people, people from the Konavle area. It belongs to Dubrovnik. However, if we go back in history, we see that the Austro-Hungarian army set up camp there a long time ago, so that none of the farmers who actually owned the land never dared bring up the issue. It is barren ground. If you go from Prevlaka towards Konavle, the ground becomes fertile. And this was the situation in the old Yugoslavia. The situation was the same in Tito's Yugoslavia, and civilians had no right to be there at all. But everyone in Herceg-Novi reckons that this was Montenegrin territory and everyone was surprised when Croats started claiming that Prevlaka belonged to Croatia. It was that far from everyone's minds during Tito's Yugoslavia that no one even considered the question, and this only cropped up when the new republics emerged. Of course, at the time, Prevlaka became ever more important, because it was considered an important strategic location at the mouth of the Boka Bay. In the Balkan mindset this became an issue of enormous importance. Montenegro and Serbia believed that the entrance to the Boka Bay should not belong to any other state but Montenegro or Serbia. If you look at the River Schelde between Belgium and the Netherlands, on the one hand you have the Belgian ship and on the other hand the Dutch ship, and no one really cares which ship is Dutch and which ship is Belgian. However, we did have a problem with this, unfortunately, I regret to say. Negotiations got off the ground, people started insulting each other after that. There was talk of war over Prevlaka. Prevlaka remained a problem for a long time, and I even dare say it is still a problem today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you have indicated that it appears that Prevlaka took on an issue of great importance. Can I ask you to clarify whether or not, at the meeting of the government that you described, where General Strugar was in attendance, on or about the 1st of October, 1991, was the issue of Prevlaka ever raised at that particular meeting as a basis for conflict? At that meeting.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been the case, but I didn't hear anything like that. I came late to the meeting, because I had seen off Mr. Wejnaendts. I wasn't aware that anyone said anything about Prevlaka that particular evening. They talked about defending the country, about liberating the area, about routing the Croats. All in all, that evening I heard nothing that -- said about Prevlaka. There were quite a number of people there; however, the meeting focussed on other things on the 1st of October. It certainly wasn't on Prevlaka. On the 3rd or 4th of October, yes, Prevlaka was back into focus, when everyone realised that there were no Ustasha entering Boka, but rather we were invading Croatia. It was then that people started saying, yes, indeed, it's all about Prevlaka, we want to liberate Prevlaka, because the Croats had taken it from us. The first evening was more about defending, but certainly also about liberating the area. That's precisely what was said. And about shattering the Croatian invasion, the Croat invaders who were allegedly trying to conquer Boka Kotorska. Later on, people started talking about liberating this area, about establishing another Dubrovnik Republic, although in my first statement dated the 2nd of October, 2002, I said that Montenegro's government did not meddle with establishing any sort of second Dubrovnik Republic. It was the national party of Montenegro. They were dreaming about establishing some sort of second Dubrovnik Republic, and they were totally involved with this. Novak Kilibarda, the president of the national party, Novak Kilibarda, was even talking about the gross national product for Dubrovnik Republic, once he is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then if -- I just want to make sure I understand you correctly. Then when you heard General Strugar speak at that meeting, are you saying he did not mention Prevlaka?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today I can't remember that he said anything about that that evening. He may have mentioned it, but his main point was that we have to defend our country from 30.000 invading Ustashe and that we needed to defeat them at a minimum cost. He said this would all be dealt with swiftly. He said this in his military way. He was talking very peacefully, and he provided the lead for everyone else at the meeting. Momir Bulatovic was his most fervent supporter, but all the others who were there, including myself, who were present, acknowledged that we needed to defend. The main point raised at the meeting was that Montenegro was under attack and that it had to be defended, that it had for defend itself. All the other issues concerning Prevlaka, conquering territory, this was all being said over the following days, but that first evening, the talk was of the defence, of the necessity to defend ourselves, and that we wouldn't allow the Ustasha to walk over us and just lie down and die. Bozo Babic reminded us of what Ustashe had done during World War II, and said that this should never be allowed to happen again. That's what was being said and that was the general atmosphere on the 1st of October, 1991, late in the evening. And this was the impression I had when I left the meeting and drove back home to Kotor. It was clear, to my mind, at least, as soon as I switched on my TV set, that there had been no invasion by any Ustasha. I had cable TV also, and I could watch foreign television programmes, international television programmes. I realised immediately that nothing like that was possible and that no Ustashe were entering Montenegro, but rather that it was the other way around, that our units were entering Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Samardzic, I'd like to ask you -- I'm so sorry. Moving on, I'd like to ask you if as a member of the cabinet, as a minister, particularly minister of foreign affairs, were you aware of any awareness at the highest levels of power in Montenegro at the time, how the conflict was affecting the Old Town of Dubrovnik? And by highest levels of power, I would include cabinet level persons, assembly-level persons, and military officials. By military, I would include TO or any other formations.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that, from the 1st of October, their idea was that they would take Dubrovnik and manage to avoid great losses or destruction. They thought this would go smoothly. Especially the top brass believed there would be no great destruction but that several days later we would be able to enjoy our coffee peacefully on the main street in Dubrovnik, as we had before. The fierce -- or the resistance that the Croats were putting up was growing. The enthusiasm on our side was dampening. Two weeks later, on the 17th of October, when Lord Carrington's plan was brought to the assembly to be speedily translated and the assembly was to continue throughout the night, the enthusiasm to liberate Dubrovnik was falling off, was decreasing, because it was clear that Dubrovnik was defending itself. And then people started talking about the need to demolish or to spare Dubrovnik. You can imagine the stories being told by extremists who were sitting in that parliament, who advocated the alleged need to invade Karlobag and Virovitica and to establish Greater Serbia. There were others yet who claimed that Montenegro should be independent, should become independent and that what was being done against Dubrovnik was a disgrace. You can imagine what the discussions were like there and the stories that people said. My own speech lasted for over an hour and a half, following which I was insulted and even hit by some people who had invaded the parliament. Those were not deputies; those were nationalists from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask you, though, going back to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going back to my more focussed question: Was there an awareness of what was happening in the area of conflict to the Old Town of Dubrovnik, the historical Old Town?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in Dubrovnik could best be conveyed by those who came back from the front. People often came back. I had never seen fighting on that scale, but many of those who had came back to Boka Kotorska. You could see that. They had with them things that they had probably looted and they passed through Boka Kotorska and Ucin [phoen]. They were talking very openly about what was being done. So people were quite well aware of what was going on, even without official reports. The official reports on Titograd TV and radio were mostly about our units gloriously shattering the Ustasha forces and liberating new areas. But certainly there were no reports of looting. The reports focussed on our forces liberating more and more ground, that they were making great progress, and that losses were low. Another thing was that people in Boka Kotorska and in the more developed parts of Montenegro had cable TV, so they could watch for themselves. They could watch Croatian TV, they could watch CNN, SkyNews, BBC, the Italian channels, Rete Uno and Rete Due, whose reporters had managed to sneak behind the lines, sneak onto the front and record what was going on there. Therefore, the people were quite well informed about what was going on, although the military administrators did their best to prevent news from spreading around the world. However, the disgrace soon became well known. I remember clearly that a meeting was once scheduled, a meeting of ambassadors in Belgrade, ambassadors from western countries. They arrived in Boka Kotorska with the intention of visiting the front line. I was supposed to come with them, but I didn't go, because I heard that Admiral Jokic would receive them and that he would not allow them as far as the front line. They would just be taken around by boat from Tivat to Herceg-Novi, to Budve and to other places which I now cannot remember. Dr. Kacic, who was also present, put this in no uncertain terms. On the one hand, the military allowed Anfilohije, the priest, to walk around the front line for days on end and spill hatred of Muslims and Croats, whereas foreign ambassadors were not allowed to go to the front and see for themselves what was happening, which is also a great shame and a great disgrace to the JNA. The priest Anfilohije, was a sworn enemy of the liberating army in World War II. He is the most important figure in the Orthodox Church in Montenegro, and he celebrated the cooperation between Drazo Mihajlovic, the Chetniks, and the German forces in World War II. Drazo Mihajlovic for them was a saint.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I wonder if I can ask you, please: Had you personally, or in your capacity as a government person, been made aware of shelling or damage on the Old Town, Stari Grad, in Dubrovnik, during this conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I as a minister did not find out about the shelling in my capacity as member of government, but I saw on TV, even Montenegrin TV was showing this, Dubrovnik being shelled. But there was smoke rising, and the allegation was that people in Dubrovnik had been burning car tyres because they wanted to show the international community that people from Dubrovnik were attacking themselves. The smoke that was rising from the town itself, they said, came from car tyres that had been set fire to, and they wanted to accuse us in the face of the international community of having attacked the town. But when I watched other TV stations, it was clear from the images that there was an attack under way, that those were no car tyres being set alight, but rather that historical monuments were specifically targeted to cause damage. So in answer to your question, yes, I was informed, and I even made video-recordings of this. I brought the tapes to Momir Bulatovic, showed him what was going on, and asked him what he believed this was. Because for a while even he was saying: They're just burning car tyres. And I said: Well, these are no car tyres being burnt. Look what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was the military reporting to the political leadership in Montenegro about what was happening in Dubrovnik, and particularly with relation to the Old Town? If you know.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military did not have much respect or consideration for us cabinet ministers. They had their so-called inner collegium [phoen], and they held meetings, and this sometimes took place in the office of Momir Bulatovic or Milo Djukanovic. So this inner cabinet composed of a few generals took place, but I don't think that all the generals took part in these meetings. Some were directly involved, some were just indirectly informed. Therefore, the government learned about the true situation only after it had all been over. I'm referring to the government as a whole. However, whether there were rumours spreading around that this or that happened, yes, there were these kind of rumours and there were one-on-one exchange of information of the looting part, for the airport, and other things. But this was not officially mentioned at the meeting, because decisions were made on the spot among ministers. We were aware of what was going on, but no true and genuine political position was taken on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was any action taken by the leadership in Montenegro to stop the attacks on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no action in that respect, except that we tried, through negotiations with Croatia, to reach at least some kind of peace and to have the army involved, included in that, in order to stop further conflicts. I don't know how this all took place. There were two or three ceasefires. The negotiations were in progress, but they were suspended, primarily because of the army. Because these ceasefires could not have been effected had not the Yugoslav army conceded to that, and it agreed under the enormous pressure of the international community, and of course they realised that there was no prospect of capturing Dubrovnik so easily and without great sacrifice, other than by trying to intensify the attacks and use more heavy artillery in order to demolish the city and the walls completely. So one of these ceasefires stipulated that the army should withdraw to Cilipi and therefore afford the citizens of Dubrovnik at least some kind of normal life. I don't remember the exact date. This ceasefire was in place for a certain period of time. The citizens of Cavtat were allowed to go to Dubrovnik. Cavtat was under occupation, but it was not destroyed, so the army allowed them to go to Dubrovnik. This kind of facilities were provided by the army in periods of time, but during the battle, they really caused tremendous damage and destruction. In my view, the arrival of Hrvoje Kacic for negotiations in Titograd on the 24th of October, 1991, who came from Zagreb with Mr. Turko, who was the Croatian MP, he landed in Titograd and he requested that the army withdraw at the distance of 16 kilometres from the Dubrovnik walls. Only myself and Risto Vukcevic received him, but everybody heard what he had to say, and eventually his request was accepted. So therefore, for a certain period of time, the army accepted and agreed to what Kacic requested for them to withdraw 16 kilometres from the walls. That did not mean that the army abandoned Konavle, just allowed, to a certain extent, for people of the town to have a normal life, because they did not have water supply, electricity supply, food. So they allowed for this period in which the army accommodated their defenders, so to say, and accepted this ceasefire. But I think that after the 16th [As interpreted] of December, it was -- the fighting was resumed. In any case, there were --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. It says 16th of December. You're giving a date. Is that 16th? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the 6th of December, because on that day there was a huge shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of what? What was shelled on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, the centre of the town was shelled from all sides, and the major damage was caused exactly on that date. Two or three days before or after - I don't remember exactly - there was a truce, and after this truce, the shelling was resumed very intensely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. A quick question. When you say "centre," are you referring to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Old Town, inside the town walls, and that is the centre of Dubrovnik. The Stradun is not the only centre of the town. That includes everything within the town walls and surrounded by the town walls. That's the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, in the twentieth century, I just wanted to ask you if you are aware of whether or not damage had occurred during this period of modern warfare, was there bombing or shelling damage that you can recall to the Old Town in the course of two world wars? If you know. The Old Town of Dubrovnik. Are you aware of any campaign that resulted in bombing or shelling the Old Town of Dubrovnik in the course of modern warfare, the twentieth century, other than what you've described here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the twentieth century, not even during the 14th century, there was never any incident of Dubrovnik being shelled or bombed. Very powerful armies of the world arrived to the walls of Dubrovnik, but that's where they stopped. That was a rule. And I can say that in 1944, when the allied forces captured Italy and when the American and British airplanes flew over the Adriatic in order to bomb the oilfields in Romania controlled by the Germans, they passed over Dubrovnik, which served as a benchmark, because they didn't have radars. A colonel of the Yugoslav Peoples Liberation Army forced our General Peko Dapcevic to send a dispatch to General Aleksandar, the commander of the Allied troops in Italy, saying: Please don't let your aircraft fly over Dubrovnik, because accidentally a bomb may drop on the town. Please have your aircraft flying to the south or to the north of Dubrovnik, but never over Dubrovnik, because it can or may be damaged. This is just a comparison, because -- a comparison between the way in which Tito's Partizans waged the war and between the soldiers of Strugar. All armies in the past did their best and refused to wage war and to target and to bomb the city of Dubrovnik. This was simply impossible for anyone to attack and demolish Dubrovnik. In the 1800s, Dubrovnik was captured by Napoleon, but without a fight. The Russian fleet of Admiral Senjanin came to attack Dubrovnik but they lowered their guns and gave up on the attack. There was not a single shell or bullet fired at Dubrovnik. That's Dubrovnik's history, and that indicates the level of the human civilisation, the level of respect afforded to Dubrovnik. What we did is the greatest shame that was done in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, if you know a person named Slavko Perovic in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's the president of the Liberal Alliance of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know what his attitude was toward the conflict in Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He was very much opposed to the attacks launched by Montenegro and the Yugoslav army on Dubrovnik. He and his whole party condemned this. They tried whatever was possible to do to prevent this. But the government and the authorities accused them of being spies and traitors and all kinds of things. But during that period, they really showed that they were honest people, which does not mean that in the later period they reversed their views to a certain extent. However, during the war against Dubrovnik, they really did credit to their party. At the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please: Are you aware of any protest rallies or gatherings in the area of Cetinje that may have occurred during the conflict? And if so, was there any participation by Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rallies, demonstrations, protests against war and against the attack on Dubrovnik in several places around Montenegro, particularly in the old capital of Cetinje, which is the most proud town in Yugoslavia, -- in Montenegro, enjoying the glory and history. And they held those rallies and demonstrations. Even though Cetinje is high above -- high up on the mountains and covered with snow, but on occasions there were between 15.000 -- 15 and 20.000 people chanting: The fairy is singing from the top, Dubrovnik, please forgive us. And that was -- this was really going to be recorded as a glorious moment of Cetinje for eternity. In addition to that, many people deserted the army, because they were just unwilling to fight. For example, Momir Bulatovic was inspecting the units, and he said: Those who don't want to fight for their homeland, let them leave the ranks. And many people did step out of the line. Many never responded to the call-up. The whole company was disbanded, and they sang that this army is not going to shoot at Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, thank you for your very full explanation. I wonder if -- I'd like to try, if we can, to finish before our break, and I note that you made reference to a phrase that you seemed to cite from folklore, perhaps, of Montenegro, of, "Forgive us Dubrovnik." I would ask to please pass around a -- distribute, please, to the Chamber and to Defence, a document which also bears that phrase. If it were also possible to request the usher to put it on the ELMO. It may be helpful. There's a copy, a copy for Mr. Samardzic as well. Thank you. Mr. Samardzic, I would ask first if you know of a person whose name appears at the bottom of what appears to be an article, a Branko Vojicic, the very last page of the article. Do you know of this person?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a journalist with the magazine Monitor. I think he's now editor in chief of Monitor. He is a very acute journalist, and unlike other journalists, he turned out to be an honest person and someone who instantly took a position against the aggression on Dubrovnik. And he condemned this. He wrote articles saying how Montenegro should behave in those difficult times. I really liked his style. However, he is very much criticised by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you this, please: You said Monitor. Is that a publication or a newspaper out of Montenegro? Just a yes or no would be helpful, so we could move along.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the magazine, a weekly paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The date on this particular article refers to 25 June 2000. And I'm going to ask you: Are you familiar with what is discussed in this article, which is a meeting which took place between President Stipe Mesic of Croatia and Milo Djukanovic, on 25 June 2000, or thereabouts? Are you familiar with the content and the facts of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I live in Australia, I just followed from afar what took place at this meeting. Otherwise, I don't know anything else. I do know the participants. I had known Mr. Bulatovic and President Mesic, and I was happy to see them meeting. And this article was written, the headline "Forgive us Dubrovnik," and that was said by Milo Djukanovic. That was a major event, not only for Montenegro but for Croatia as well. After all, the suffering, the war, it is good that we have this kind of reconciliation, and I think that it is very good that this journalist wrote this article. No matter how critical he was of Mr. Djukanovic, he praised what he did in Cavtat, and he believes that this will contribute to establishing completely new relations between Montenegro and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, in relation to some of the items that came out of the meeting, and also what Mr. Djukanovic had to say, I would turn your attention to the very bottom of the first page of this. And I will simply ask you if this -- if you are aware of this particular aspect of the discussion. In this way, Djukanovic unmasked the whole scenario. He explicitly admitted that the "liberation" of Dubrovnik had not been undertaken because the Ustasha had attacked Montenegro (interpretation of General Strugar and Djukanovic himself at the time), nor for "reasons of humaneness" in order to unblock the military barracks and protect the "threatened Serbs" in Dubrovnik region (according to Branko Kostic and Defence Minister of Montenegro, Babic) nor "because of fascism", and Kadijevic's "war trap" (Momir Bulatovic). But that the war had been waged for Greater Serbia. Does this explanation about no Ustasha attacking Montenegro, is it consistent with your understanding or your belief of what the real state of affairs was at the time of the meeting in October 1991, at which you heard General Strugar speak of an Ustasha attack? And I use the term in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From these few lines said by President Djukanovic in Cavtat, it is clear that the policy that had been initiated on the 1st of October, 1991 had been completely unmasked. We were never attacked by the Ustasha, which Djukanovic states very explicitly. There was no need to liberate Dubrovnik. There was no need to rout any Ustasha, because there were no Ustasha around. There was no need to wage a war for peace, because there was no war with Dubrovnik. There was no war trap, as Kadijevic claimed, that there weren't 30.000 Ustasha around. Milo Djukanovic's admission in Cavtat helped to show clearly the true nature of the criminal policy of the JNA, Serbia and Montenegro towards Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Samardzic, one other point I'd like to ask you about: On the first page, in the middle of the second complete paragraph -- on the first page, in the middle of the second complete paragraph, starting with the sentence, after the word "Cavtat,": "And as concerning the crimes committed under the walls of Dubrovnik, Djukanovic said that the responsibility had to be personalised, that it was the only and the best way to lift the mortgage of national responsibility, which was through history imputed, or at least there was an attempt to do it, to the Croat people, and nowadays there was an attempt to impute it to the Montenegrin people." Having published that, are you aware, looking back from 1991, after the conflict - I'm sorry - after the damage on the Old Town, are you aware of any discipline that may have been imposed on any of the military persons involved in the Dubrovnik campaign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I'm aware of. I don't think a single military official, to the best of my knowledge, was ever called to account for their actions in and around Dubrovnik. There's quite a lot of work to be done there, but it seems that nothing has so far been undertaken. Maybe some people were awarded higher ranks, but I don't think anyone was ever called to account over Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, briefly, I think because we have to resort to the use of a real video, and it's a very brief one. I'm sorry. I'd ask to have this item moved into evidence, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P32.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it were possible to present at least the opening part of a video, and to distribute a transcript of this video. If the Chamber would allow, I'd like to try to really conclude within the next few minutes, if that would be possible. If it were possible to ask our colleagues in the audiovisual section to run it. And I'll try to get my points across very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can we stop for one minute? Can you just point out, please, who is who in this particular video, just the personalities, who is President Mesic and who is President Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Mesic, Stjepan Mesic, is the president of the Republic of Croatia. President Milo Djukanovic was at the time the president of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now he is the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right. Who is the person with the beard in this video? The person with the beard. If you could show us who is President Mesic and who is President Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one with the beard, that's President Mesic. And the one sitting next to him, the tall one, that's President Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And there was a mention of the place Cavtat. Does this meeting -- is this the meeting that is ascribed in the "Forgive Us Dubrovnik" article?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's at a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Stop for one second. I'd just like to turn the Chamber's attention to the -- and I don't believe the interpreters maybe have been given a copy. We're now looking at, on the first page, the third complete paragraph, where Mr. Djukanovic is explaining the purpose of the particular session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. It would certainly be possible to go through the whole video, if the Chamber wishes to do so, but I think perhaps in the interests of time, if it would be permissible to leave -- we will have it submitted correctly. Unfortunately, Sanction has limited us. But if we could ask for both the transcript and the video to be assigned a number, we will then substitute what our original is with a proper copy and provide the entire document, as it were - sorry, the entire video, or a portion that we have in the original, to the Chamber. We'll provide our original, sorry. But I'm terribly sorry about the situation with Sanction this morning; it couldn't be helped. If the Chamber is minded to do so, we would ask that this exhibit be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The video and the transcript will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be Prosecution Exhibit P33, and the transcript, P33.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution has no further questions. Thank you for your patience on letting us finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Somers. We propose now to adjourn for 20 minutes for a break, and we'll then resume. An opportunity for a little break, Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The cross-examination should now commence. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However, before I start my cross-examination, I would like to point out something very important. When this witness was announced by the OTP, the estimate was that the examination-in-chief would last between two and three hours. In spite of that, the examination-in-chief effectively, questions and answers, lasted for four hours and ten minutes, which is significantly longer in relation to their original estimate. What I wish to point out, in view of the remaining time, and especially in view of the effective session of question and answers, and the large number of questions asked by the OTP, and this witness is equally important for us as for the OTP, I can now immediately inform the Honourable Chamber that I will not be able to finish my cross-examination today, in view of the many open issues and the considerable significance of everything that has been said in this courtroom during this witness's testimony. Of course, I'm aware of the comments that have been made to the Defence team in relation to situations where our cross-examination was longer than the examination-in-chief. However, we do not believe that these general guidelines can always be strictly complied with. Sometimes the OTP believes that they will take up less time questioning a witness than it turns out to be, and sometimes there can be sudden and unexpected situations that arise during a witness's examination. What I wish to say is that this witness is a very material witness to our case, and I don't think I will have enough time today to finish my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that indication, Mr. Rodic. We do see that the time taken in the course of the evidence in chief of the witness is longer than was anticipated, and we will bear that in mind as you proceed. Perhaps you could move into your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Samardzic, good morning. My name is Goran Rodic, attorney at law from Podgorica, appearing on behalf of General Strugar. On behalf of General Strugar, I will ask you questions to do with your prior testimony. First of all, can I please have the usher's assistance, if the ELMO could be removed, so I that could have direct eye contact with the witness. Mr. Samardzic, my first question to you is: Before coming to the Tribunal and prior to the start of your testimony, did you provide any written statements to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did provide a written statement. I believe in the year of 2000, that was three and a half years ago, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Allow me to remind you. I'm looking at the first page of your statement. Is it true that it was on the 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, and 23rd of October, 2000?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the course of your answers to the Prosecutor's questions, we heard a brief history of your life. However, I don't think this issue was raised, and I do think you testified about this in your statement. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether, in the course of your career, in the course of your life, in relation to the territory of Montenegro, where you lived and worked for a long time, did you ever suffer any persecutions, personally? If so, please, what was the reason? If you could please elucidate.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was still quite young, I faced difficulty because my father had been awarded a medal of courage by the Partizans army. He fought fascism since 1941. In 1948 he was accused in connection with the inform bureau resolution. This was not true, however. My father was arrested and sent to Goli Otok penitentiary. A son of someone who was on Goli Otok could not have a normal life in Montenegro at that time. This person would face many problems, and it would be very hard for this person to assert him or herself. And this was the situation I faced throughout my education.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that throughout your education, and when you found a job afterwards, you were facing great problems, great adversity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, initially there were problems. Afterwards, however, people realised that I was no enemy, that I was an honourable man, and those problems ceased to exist. My further development was smooth and normal. However, initially I did face great difficulty. One year they wouldn't allow me to enroll in the maritime school. They believed that, as a sailor, I had no right to travel abroad, being the son of an inform bureau person. Later they allowed me to travel abroad, but the issue was brought up whether I should be allowed to sail abroad or not. You could sail along the Adriatic Coast without leaving the Yugoslav territory. Also there was the Jugolinija, where you travelled abroad. I was allowed to join Jugolinija, and for my career to develop. I soon became the youngest president, the youngest manager ever in that company. I was the youngest sea master in the entire Yugoslavia at that time. So yes, initially there was trouble, there was difficulty. Afterwards, this trouble, this difficulty, disappeared, thanks to my own work and effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did these problems cause you to look for a job in Croatia after your schooling because you were not given a job in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it was because I was not able to get a job in Montenegro. I did, as a matter of fact, get a job in Montenegro. My first job was with Jugooceanija, as an apprentice. Once my apprenticeship was over, I was given a job with Jugolinija, because there were no vacancies in Jugooceanija. And it was in Jugolinija that I was first promoted. When I was 25, I was first mate, and when I was 27 I was the commander of the ship.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste any more time with this. As early as 1974, you worked for Jugooceanija, in Kotor. At that time, the director of Jugooceanija retired. As far as I know, you were proposed, your name was put forward to replace him as the manager, general, of Jugooceanija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there something that prevented you from taking up that position at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not personally prevented, but people believed it was still a bit too early for me to become the manager of Jugooceanija, and I was appointed an MP in the Yugoslav parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss that later. My answer [As interpreted] now is specifically about the first period after the manager retired and before the new manager was appointed.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were saying that I should perhaps be appointed manager. But it wasn't only me. Whenever a new manager was appointed, Mr. Rodic, there are several candidates, and I was among those candidates. Eventually, I was not appointed. Another more senior person, Bokcevic, was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, on page 3 of your statement you said: "However, the Montenegrin Communist Party opposed my appointment. They still viewed me as the son of a traitor and thus unworthy of promotion." That's what you told the investigators; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that was precisely the statement that I made. There was something like that. People believed that it was still a bit too early for me to become a manager, and yes, I was the son of a man whom they considered as a traitor. Therefore, I was not appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you go through your statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I don't believe that what you're saying now is particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, can you just answer my questions. This will keep us from wasting time, because we don't have much time on our hands right now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please be reminded not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... For some order here. You are each interrupting each other, and each of you is jumping in ahead of the translation. You are well aware of the needs of the translator for pauses between questions and answers. But more importantly, of course, when a question is asked, Mr. Samardzic, if you'd be kind enough to answer that question, and you obviously understand the question. You should be able to answer that question. And that will then enable Mr. Rodic to move on to his next question. If there are matters that concern you, they can be raised by -- later in the hearing by questions in re-examination by Ms. Somers. Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. What I want to achieve is to have brief answers to my questions, which will expedite our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, this wasn't something I made up. I simply read the first passage on page 3 of your statement where this is stated, and that's why I asked you whether you had gone through your statement before signing it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did read the statement before I signed it, and that's precisely why I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You placed your signature there because you believed that the statement accurately reflected your words during the interview, I assume.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of errors, which we promptly corrected. But if you insist: My choice in 1974 -- or rather, my appointment as general director, probably there were a number of factors contributing to this, as well as the ones that you have referred to. I was the son of a man who was considered a traitor, and probably people said he can't become manager. I'm not trying to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My opinion is quite different, and I will tell you why.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After finding a job with Jugolinija, you made headway very quickly. You became a manager in that company, and in 1974 you got a job with Jugooceanija. In 1970, you attended a course in maritime transport, in management, under the aegis for the UN conference for trade development in Geneva, while you still had a job with Jugooceanija. Once you completed the course, you were invited to go back to Jugooceanija headquarters and work there as a commercial administrator, processing bills from all over the world. In, 1974 you were promoted to become port captain, and later you became the maritime supervisor. In 1974, the League of Communists, of which you were a member, appointed you a deputy to the Yugoslav Assembly. In 1978, your term of office expired and you were appointed as president of the association for self-management in foreign trade in Montenegro, where you spent four years. Towards the end of 1982, you were appointed a representative of the Yugoslav Chamber of commerce in Australia, and in June 1983 you took up your post in Sydney. Five years later, having lived in Sydney for five years, you went to Brisbane, where you helped organise the Expo in 1988. Early 1989, you returned to Montenegro. On the 9th of May, 1989, soon after your return, you were appointed director of Jugooceanija. In November of the same year, you were elected deputy to the Montenegrin Assembly at the first free general elections in Montenegro. You were an appointee of the League of Communists, which soon changed its name into Democratic Socialist Party. In July 1990, you were appointed as a representative of Montenegro to the Federal Chamber of the Republics. In February 1991, you were elected foreign minister in Montenegro's government, the Prime Minister was Milo Djukanovic, and you held on to your post as deputy in the assembly and your post as manager for Jugooceanija, which means that you had three positions at the same time. In 1992, if I'm not mistaken, in May, on the 26th of May, 1992, you resigned as foreign minister. You stepped down. On the 8th of June, 1992, you moved with your family to Malta, due to the sanctions that had been imposed, and from Malta you could run the activities of the company of which you were the manager, Jugooceanija. As far as all the positions that I've enumerated, is the list correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There appears to be no question put to the witness, but rather a narration of the statement. And if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's just been a question put about the whole list: Is it correct?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, your question was: "Is all of that correct?" Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, what you read is correct, with a few exceptions that you added. I wasn't appointed, as you said, by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I must interrupt you. Please listen. There is no mention of the party in my enumeration of your posts, except that you were a candidate put forward by the League of Communists, that soon after that, it changed its name into the Democratic Party of Socialists. So I never, ever mentioned the Communist Party in that context. What I want to hear is whether this information contained in your c.v. are correct. If there is something that is incorrect, please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when you say "appointed," it is well known who appoints people. When you speak in that manner, it is sometimes understood that people are appointed by the Communist Party. That was not the case in my life. Even some dates are wrong. It is true that I attended in 1974 a specialised course held by UNCDAT. So you made a mistake by four years. And the difference is that after 1970, I got a job with Jugooceanija in Kotor, and before that time I sailed on ships. These were not very significant differences, but since you insist on details, I felt it was necessary to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I accept that I perhaps may have quoted a wrong year. But in your statement, it says that you took the course in Geneva in 1970.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But basically, all these functions are part of your c.v.?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look at the sequence and how they occurred, it wasn't according to the usual practice that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia. For instance, I was not appointed the director by the party but on a referendum by the workers, which was totally contrary to the opinion of the party committee. And when I was appointed the manager -- the director of Jugooceanija in 1989, the party was against it. But my point is that whatever you read here has another side of the coin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were any other people similar to you that were branded in the same manner who were removed from their positions and quite simply could not advance in their careers due to being attributed the same things that had been attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. It was particularly difficult for me in my early youth, because they didn't know what I was going to do. So on two occasions I was banned from attending the school. I was expelled in Cetinje. In the fourth year I was expelled from some other schools as well. You didn't read that. And that was only because my father was at Goli Otok. And one really needed strength to go through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But tell me: Do you know any other case that people were accused of similar things and who managed to achieve such a career as you did? Can you give us a few examples?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact number. There were lots of them. There were other people who faced difficulties but later on were accepted. The situation in Yugoslavia was such that you first become punished and rejected, and then they accept you. You know very well that that was the system in Yugoslavia. They could never pin it on me that I was in favour of inform bureau [As interpreted]. They would always say that I was the son of a man

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I think that -- I think you're rather exaggerating your position and all the obstacles that you had faced in your early youth, given the fact that you discharged very important functions and positions in Montenegro and Yugoslavia. You said that you were away from Montenegro for nearly five and a half years, up until 1989, when you returned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in July 1992 you left Montenegro again?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In June 1992 I left for Malta. I returned in July to meet the UK foreign secretary, and I spent two days in Belgrade at the invitation of Milo Djukanovic, and then after that I returned to Malta again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So since July 1992, up until today, you have been -- you have not been living in Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I visited Montenegro in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you come to live and work in Montenegro or you just visited?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you can qualify that. Up until 1994, I was the director of Jugooceanija, and during all this period I was in Malta, but I came often to Kotor, to the company headquarters, because the majority of the offices were in Kotor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Between 1994 and 2004, have you been living in Montenegro [As interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what are you doing in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a pensioner, as far as Yugoslavia is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I must point out that the translation and what has been on the screen appear not to be in sync. The question was: "Between --" on line 17, page 42, "Between 1994 and 2000," [sic] I believe the question was, "Have you been living outside Montenegro," and it shows, "Living in Montenegro."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I asked the witness whether between 1994 and 2004 he has been living outside Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can I hear your answer again?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the -- after I was dismissed from Jugooceanija in 1994, I continued living in Malta for a certain period of time, and then I moved in Australia, where I live now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you regularly follow the developments in Yugoslavia, which is now called Serbia and Montenegro, and before that the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I surf the Internet, I receive newspapers, and I'm fully informed of what's happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I presume, then, that after you resigned from the position of the foreign minister, you also followed the events in Yugoslavia through newspapers or through your occasional visits, when you used to come to Kotor while you were still working for Jugooceanija.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I followed the events, as far as it was possible. Of course, I wasn't very close or a part of the top leadership, but whatever other ordinary people could find out, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Given the time distance between now and these events in 1991 and 1992, when you are testifying today, do you see any difference between your conduct and your way of thinking and acting in the period 1991 and 1992, and now, or do you that nothing has changed in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my way of thinking and my attitude towards the events that took place in Yugoslavia, nothing has changed. I could never accept the events that took place in Yugoslavia, as many did, qualifying it as the defence of Yugoslavia. I rather thought that that was a tremendous disgrace and that we were making -- doing terrible evil that Montenegro was involved in, and that's what I think today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you appear as the witness in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2002, about one and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you are following the situation in the former Yugoslavia, and particularly in Montenegro, were there any reactions in Montenegro after you gave testimony at this trial, and do you know what these reactions were?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you rebut any of those reactions, or did you make any statements?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although it is difficult to rebut anything. It was a terrible attack on my person. It would have taken me 20 days to write all the rebuttals to whatever was written in the press about me, and apart from so many ugly things, there were some good things written about me. Part of the press agreed with me, but most of the press, particularly from Belgrade, attacked me. And I think it would have been better if I had ignored that, but I didn't. I responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you attacked by anyone from the Montenegrin press?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Chetnik daily Dan launched such a fierce attack on me. I don't think it's worth mentioning, although maybe it might be necessary, because unbelievable lies were written in this newspaper Dan, which is renowned for its lies and made-up stories. I follow this on a regular basis. I try to write rebuttals. They did publish some of my articles, not all of them, but they did publish them nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, tell me: Do you face any problems in Montenegro, or was it because of business or some other reasons that you decided not to live in Montenegro any more?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are no particular problems. There is the problem of Jugooceanija. The company that I used to run, it's been destroyed, and I'm convinced that while I was at the helm of the company, I did my job well, that I should have gotten recognition after that. However, certain parts of the government who wanted to grab Jugooceanija for them -- Jugooceanija used to be the company that had 22 ocean liners. It survived the sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
