utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Let us not waste any more time on this. Does that mean, if I understand you properly, that your problem with Montenegro is related to what you just said, because of this former company of Jugooceanija?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My problem concerning Jugooceanija exists, because Jugooceanija is located in Kotor and there are many people who think, unrightly, that I was the blame for what happened to Jugooceanija. It's been ten years since then, and in that period, Jugooceanija went down the drain, and I left it with 17 ships.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been called to account for that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody did that, except for certain newspapers, like Dan, who dig out some journalists and seamen who write lies and provocations about men. However, never I was ever held accountable officially for what I did [As interpreted]. This was just hearsay and rumours by people who could have properly been paid or not paid to do this, spread these rumours and lies. But as far as the official policy is concerned, the government, the trade unions, never found anything wrong, because I think I was very successful as the manager of this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if the official authorities do not question your responsibility, what is then the reason that you cannot go to Montenegro? Because I presume you have some extended family there.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who told you that I cannot go to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You just told me that your living abroad is connected with the problems that you have in Montenegro concerning Jugooceanija.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that does not mean that I cannot go there. I simply don't want to face any unpleasant situation with people who are accusing me about the fate of that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let us now proceed to another area of questioning. I suppose that at the time when you worked and lived in the former SFRY, and when you entered the political arena and took the position of the foreign minister, you knew the constitution of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I did. I was even involved in drawing up the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just SFRY, not FRY. They should make this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you know probably the federal laws that were in force in that period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact when the new Croatian constitution was promulgated? I am referring to the one -- to the period directly preceding these events.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose in 1990. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did this constitution -- was this constitution in conformity with the SFRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Based on that constitution, which, if you don't know, I can confirm was in contradiction with the then-SFRY constitution -- so did Croatia establish its armed forces under this constitution?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They started forming their armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the question: Under the SFRY constitution, which were the only legal armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Anything contrary to that could be dubbed as paramilitary forces within the state governed by the law?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, provided there's not a new state that emerged. However, a new state of Croatia emerged in the meantime. So that is the foundation of all the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Croatia established its own state, then presumably it should establish its armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, when was it that Croatia established its own state?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it proclaimed its independence from other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, on the 13th of May, 1990. Sorry. 30th of May. And then the parliament adopted a declaration. I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. That was on the 25th and 26th of June, 1991, the parliament of Croatia declared independence from the rest of Yugoslavia. Before that date, was Croatia establishing its own armed forces? Was it working on that? And were those paramilitary places already -- paramilitary forces already in place there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was some police unit in Croatia, in Borovo Selo and other places. But as for the Croatian army, I don't know if it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about the National Guard Corps? And if you did, when was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about the National Guard Corps about that period, but I didn't believe or consider that to be some kind of new army. Just like we had territorial forces in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What you heard about the emergence of the National Guard Corps refers to the period before the declaration of independence, and that is before June 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, because at the time I was more focussed on relations with Dubrovnik, as the manager of Jugooceanija, with Belgrade, and I did not notice any members of the National Guard Corps in Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that this notwithstanding, the first half of 1991, in addition to being an economist, you also became a minister with Montenegro's government, minister of foreign affairs. You were also a deputy to the parliament. All these things I'm asking you about, even outside your activity, in your official political capacity, these things were widely debated. They were very much issues in the public eye at the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not the way you're putting it to me now. There were certain things. Please allow me. I attended meetings of the federal assembly, being a deputy to the Chamber of the republics. There were certain problems with this, but not to the extent that a war should break out. There were certain units emerging, but not only in Croatia; it was like that all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, first of all, I'm not trying to insinuate anything. My question is very specific. You have the right to answer my question. I would like to avoid political debate here, and I would like you to answer my specific questions with very specific and to-the-point answers, without elucidating too much. We are in no position to exchange views and opinions now. We are in a position only to exchange specific questions and answers. My question is: Did you know about the National Guard Corps being set up prior to the 25th of June, 1991? Briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about certain units being set up but back then I did not realise that a Croatian army was being set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. During your work in that period, did you hear anything about the Croatian Party of Rights, about Dobrosav Paraga, about Ante Djapic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about their own armed formations set up by the party itself?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of their armed units. I knew about their activities and I knew they were working along Ustasha lines, that they were advocating the Ustasha ideology. They were the extreme right. I was aware of that and I condemned it. But I didn't believe they were posing any great danger to Yugoslavia as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question was not about your views on them being a danger or not. I'm asking you specifically about --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. They did exist. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the heritage of that party, what the guidelines are and what the propaganda was at the time espoused by the party.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows the ideology of Ante Starcevic, and that's precisely why it's called the Croatian Party of Rights. It advocates an independent Croatian state and secession from the Serbs. It espouses all the nationalistic views that were espoused by the Ustasha in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this in any way related to Ante Pavelic and the independent state of Croatia from World War II?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are related.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which side were Ante Pavelic and the independent state of Croatia on in World War II?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Pavelic sided with Hitler's Germany and fascist Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We agree that throughout 1990 and 1991, Paraga was promoting his own party platform and the heritage the party had included his idols or role models from World War II?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this may be correct, but I don't think they were a force to be reckoned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will ask you this question when we consider your role as a military expert. Then you can give us your opinion about how strong or how much of a menace a certain party may have been. However, that is not my question for the time being. Regardless, and I do not wish now to enter a debate about their force. You have the party setting up an armed unit. Can this be legal at all at the time in the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, with the constitution that was in place and with the JNA as the only legal armed force in the country?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should not be viewed as legal, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that at a meeting of the SFRY presidency on the 11th of December, 1990, reports were presented for the first time on paramilitary weapons being brought into Croatia, extra mobilisation of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and weapons being handed out to the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it on the news about something like this being done. I'm not familiar with any details, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the information published by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence on the setting up of illegal paramilitary units in the SFRY, a well argumented report indicating that in Croatia, work was under way, very much in establishing an armed force in order to threaten the legal state of Yugoslavia, and that for this purpose they were obtaining large amounts of illegal weapons and ammunition in December 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that. I knew about the Serbian Krajina being set up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the speakers please be reminded not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you watch TV? Did you read the press? During your work in parliament, and as a member of the government, did you ever hear anything about this going on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an MP at the time, and this was certainly not presented in the parliament the way you make it out to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you perhaps watch TV programmes where a film was shown on the illegal import of weapons from Hungary into the Republic of Croatia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a film like that. But I saw different films.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a continuing problem, Mr. Rodic. You ask a question. You may be getting an answer that is not what you are expecting, but you are butting in over the answer. I think you must allow the answer to come, and if it's not the answer to your question, then repeat your question until you get the answer you are looking for. But we can't have this continuing -- your speaking over the witness. It becomes impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. However, I'm trying to achieve the following: Specific question, specific answer. However, once having provided a specific answer, the witness just goes off on a tangent, providing testimony that has nothing to do with my original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm conscious of the issue, Mr. Rodic, and if it goes too much, I will raise it directly with the witness. But at the moment, I think the balance is in favour of you waiting until you've had the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the dispatch from the Presidency dated the 9th of January, 1991, talking about the amassing of illegal weapons and setting up of paramilitary units, thereby creating conditions for armed conflict and inter-ethnic conflict of great proportions, which would greatly endanger the safety of citizens and the existence of the state of SFRY itself?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this. But this did not only apply to Croatian paramilitary units, but rather to all paramilitary units emerging at the time. We're talking about the general framework of the disintegration of Yugoslavia, and everyone was ready to undermine Yugoslavia. Everyone was preparing for that, not only Croatia. Croatia was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, but was Croatia involved in this too?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You're certain about the others, however, but you merely assume when we talk about Croatia.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't insinuate. I only said so because I was not sure about any of them, not with sure and certain knowledge. I knew that nationalism was on the rise throughout Yugoslavia at that time, and many different sides were working on undermining the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia set out to establish an independent state? Was that part of the platform of the party in power at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Croatia wanted to secede. If you have the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Community in mind, their platform was to secede from Yugoslavia, but in compliance with the constitution that was then in place. The existing constitution then allowed for the possibility of secession, not only for Croatia but for all the republics of Yugoslavia. Self-determination and secession. They were entitled to this under the constitution. The fact that it came to blows and that weapons were used is a different story altogether, but this was allowed under the constitution. I mean secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Whose right was it to, the right to self-determination and secession under the constitution?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right of each and every republic within the state. Each and every republic had the same right. Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Slovenia, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you: Did it say each and every republic or each and every people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. The republic and the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Having ascertained through your answer to one of my previous questions that the new constitution of the Republic of Croatia was not in conformity with the federal constitution, how, then, can there be any form of legal secession, secession that was still legal? This can in no way be in conformity with the provisions of the SFRY constitution governing these issues.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, but the fact that something is not in conformity with something else does not immediately make it illegal. Not in conformity does not mean that it's illegal or against the constitution. The Croatian constitution was not in conformity with the SFRY constitution, which still falls far short of making it illegal. I am not familiar now with the details of the relevant provisions, because it's been a long time and I have not dealt with this, but I do know that Croatia, not only Croatia, but rather every republic, had the right to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So how exactly did Croatia go about this initially?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, it was peaceful; and after that, it escalated into a full-blown war, because self-managing units or regions were being formed and then conflict broke out, armed conflict, war. In a situation like that, it was only to be expected that legal norms would no longer be complied with and that weapons would speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you determine the period of time, or rather, the way in which Croatia launched this initiative, how it all started and how the whole thing was done, how Croatia tried to implement its right to secession?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a referendum, as far as I remember. There was a referendum in Croatia, a referendum about self-determination and secession, about the creation of an independent state. Most of the Croatian people, and even most of the Serbs living in Croatia, the way I've been informed, voted in favour of an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to argue with you on this point. But even so, was there, under the constitution of the SFRY, any other procedure that needed to be complied with?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The federal assembly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So was this complied with?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the Presidency of the SFRY passed an order, on the 9th of January, 1991, that all armed units that were not part of the unified armed units of the SFRY or organs of the Ministry of the Interior were to be disarmed, and that were not legal under the federal law? Further stating that all equipment and weapons should be handed over to the nearest JNA units within ten days?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember no such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You don't remember that the presidency took any steps like this, even if you can't specifically remember the wording of the order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were meetings and sessions, but which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The 9th of January, 1991. That's what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th of January, 1991, I can't remember. I know there were problems surrounding this, but I forgot about this order being passed. I knew there were problems about weapons and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to refresh your memory. This order was not actually carried out within the next ten days, that's by the 19th of January, but Croatia officially requested an extension of this deadline by 48 hours, for this to be done by the 21st of January. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that once this deadline expired, 21st of January, the Republic of Croatia raised the combat readiness of the entire MUP troops and the National Guard Corps and that the Supreme Command Staff reciprocated by raising the combat readiness of all its units in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It strikes me as strange that you shouldn't remember these things. These were after all important developments for Montenegro as well as for the other parts of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should that matter to Montenegro? What is it that occurred in Montenegro at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you view Montenegro as a unit that was isolated from the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means. It was by no means an isolated part. But can you please repeat what exactly you claim happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Once this other extended deadline expired, the 48-hour extension for disarming all illegal military units in SFRY territory, the Republic of Croatia, on the 21st of January, raised the combat readiness of all MUP forces and National Guard Corps, while the Supreme Command Staff reciprocated by taking the same measure, for the JNA units that were stationed in the Republic of Croatia. Are you familiar with that? Is this how it happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I remember there were problems about that, to do with that, but I don't remember these specific developments that you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1991, which means most definitely before the events that you testified to here occurring in the area of Dubrovnik, so prior to these events, do you know, were there any blockades of the JNA's barracks, attacks on the military installations and facilities and members of the JNA in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were those -- were there many attacks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But as far as I know, this took place in Varazdin, Osijek. Yeah, there were several cases in which the JNA barracks were blocked in certain parts of Croatia. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the situation the same in the capital of Croatia, Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Zagreb. I knew that there were problems, but I don't know there were any blockades in Zagreb. The whole convoys of the JNA, troops and weapons, passed through Zagreb en route from Slovenia, and they were not detained there. But what else happened in Zagreb, I don't know. However, I know that in other towns, these incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Due to the blockades and attacks on the JNA, did the JNA suffer any tragic consequences and material damage to their facilities and equipment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were people who were killed. There was equipment and facilities damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you mention these military convoys being relocated, were there any attacks on those convoys and the seizure of weapons from there while they passed through Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some delays of these convoys, but I don't think there were any major attacks on them. They were just stopped or detained. However, they passed through to Serbia and Bosnia, and also they travelled by sea, for instance, on the ship "ST. STEPHEN", the army troops from Pilan and Kopir, in Slovenia, withdrew and arrived in Boka. Yes, there were such cases that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Croatian paramilitary units, and later the armed forces of this republic, took part, or rather, crossed over to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to join the battle there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about 1992, but yes, in 1993. In 1993, they entered Bosnia, while the war was there in full swing, because the war in Bosnia started in 1992. At that time, the Croatian army did not participate in the conflict. But they did take part in conflict since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, was the Croatian army involved in war operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the BH army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is irrelevant to the issues surrounding 1991, and I'd ask that we stay focussed on the scope of direct, or at least within the temporal period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, is there any particular purpose that you pursue this? I know that you have earlier dealt with matters that are directly relevant, but this does seem to be getting well away from the issues important to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do understand this intervention by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, and by yourself as well. It's not my place to evaluate the accurateness of the answers concerning certain information -- information allocation given by this witness. I just want to highlight how the issue of military troops and territories were intertwined in his testimony and in his answers to the Prosecutor's questions. I think this is very relevant, because during his testimony, at the time mentioned in the witness testimony, the Republic of Croatia established its paramilitary forces and whether any such actions were minimised or totally covered up through the answers given to the Prosecutor. If the opposite was the case, then we shall try to prove that. If I may ask one more question regarding the previous theme, and then I will proceed with another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm continuing my objection. 1993 references are utterly irrelevant. The time period, I submit, should be really restricted to the time period involved in the indictment, on this particular issue, unless there is some really significant impact, which has not been, in my view, articulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you may ask one more question on this theme, and then I will ask you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will comply with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Concerning the period that you mentioned that the Croatian paramilitary formations were involved in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, my very short question is: Was Croatia in any way threatened or attacked by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order for its actions to be warranted in terms of sending its troops to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that Croatia was threatened by Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, there was an excuse for that, as far as I understood at the time. Their intention was to protect the Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us proceed. Do you know that the president of the Republic of Croatia at the time that we are discussing now, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, on the 24th of May, 1992, at a rally on the Ban Jelacic Square - I said on the 24th of May, 1992 - convened to celebrate the anniversary of independence? He said, and I quote: There would not be any war had Croatia not wished to have the war. But we judge that our only way towards independence was war. Therefore, we conducted political negotiations, while at the same time we were establishing our own armed units. Had we not done that in that way, we would not have achieved our goal. Therefore, the war could only have been avoided had we abandoned our main objective, and that is the independence of the state of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this speech, and especially I don't know anything about this politicising of the issues that -- I don't think that the president of Croatia -- I think that the president of Croatia seems to have said that Croatia would not have gained independence without conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So let us not dwell any further on that. Have you heard the name of Hrvoje Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about Mr. Hrvoje Sarinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was an advisor to President Tudjman. And in the Croatian cabinet and he had some other positions, but he was a very important figure who negotiated with Slobodan Milosevic and with the Serbian side. He was a very active Croatian politician of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about his statements regarding the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina between the two aforementioned presidents?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read something about the agreement between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic, about how to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I personally don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You often mentioned your friend, if I understand you properly - and correct me if I'm wrong - Hrvoje Kacic. Can you tell us if that is correct? And if it is, what was he involved in at the time? What did he do at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was the president of the parliamentary commission for foreign policy. He was also the professor at the Zagreb University. He was born in Dubrovnik. We met when we were young men. We were both in swimming, in sports. And I think he was a very correct person who was very benevolent concerning Montenegro. He was not a communist. He didn't want to become part of the Communist Party. He consistently advocated his views that throughout his life he was fighting for an independent state of Croatia, and he made no secret of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you acquainted with the former president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met him a few times in The Hague during the peace conference on Yugoslavia. I met him in Igalo, in Montenegro, when I hosted his meeting with Milosevic on the 16th of September, 1991, before the outbreak of hostilities. And that's about all. I met him only officially, a few times. And the same applies to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any private contacts with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't qualify that as private contacts. If you are referring to a separate meeting between Momir Bulatovic and myself, on one side, and President Tudjman and Minister Separovic on the other, people qualified this as a private meeting because we did not inform President Milosevic. We had a meeting with President Tudjman on the issue of Prevlaka, and that took place either during a break or after the conference in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did President Tudjman, during the last conference in The Hague, approach you and greet you, and did you exchange some greetings or did you have any conversation at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always greeted President Tudjman, without fail, and this last time was particularly friendly, was because President Tudjman greeted me warmly when he heard that I was a relative of Jovan Baldani, also a university professor in Zagreb, and Baldani, while he was a student, he visited Tudjman when he was in prison. And he just reminded me of that, because Jovan Baldani and I are very close relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why was Tudjman in prison at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably because he advocated the independent state of Croatia. He was an army general who did not agree with the policy pursued at the time. He was convicted. But in any case, he was in prison because of his nationalistic views.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when he was in prison?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in late 1950s or early 1960s. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that, especially at that time, which was very close to the end of the Second World War, and having a JNA general involved, was this kind of his activity contrary to the heritage of this national -- Peoples Liberation War?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't qualify him as an enemy of the heritage of the peoples liberation struggle. His father and his brother were killed by the Ustashe. He was also awarded the medal for bravery and valour during the war as a Partizan. However, if he had certain views about the status of Croatia, he was not pursuing the idea of creating some new, independent state of Croatia, but rather a new democratic Croatia that would secede from Yugoslavia and exist like that. I'm not saying that he was not guilty and convinced accordingly, but I would never qualify him as an Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I never mentioned the term "Ustasha."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you are -- your questions are leading to this. Tudjman fought for an independent state of Croatia in his own way, with his ideology. We need not accept this, but we should not spit on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you see me, or do you answer my question in fear that I'm trying to lead you to something? I'm just asking you very specific questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I am not afraid of anything. I am not a coward, so I have no fears from you, but that you are leading me in a certain way, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Rodic, we might interrupt the debate there, and we will have a 20-minute break. And it may be possible for you to just continue with your cross-examination afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, in relation to my last question before the break, I'll repeat it for you. Mr. Tudjman's activity as a general of the JNA, was it contrary to the common struggle of the Yugoslav peoples and the tradition of the liberation struggle and the creation of a unified state?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's no indication of what a common struggle is. This is a term that has not been defined, and I would ask that the question be narrowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to rephrase my question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The SFRY, was it created as a result of the common struggle of the Yugoslav peoples and based on the tradition of the liberation struggle?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The common struggle of the peoples, including their right to secession and self-determination. This was set down at the second session of the AVNOJ, and this was still valid until the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: General Tudjman's activity throughout the period, was it then legal?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what specifically President Tudjman did in that period of time, but I believe he had the right to fight in a legal way for Croatia's independence. If that's what he did, then he was perfectly entitled to it. But I don't know what he was tried for, and not knowing that, I can't tell you whether he was tried for reasons fair or unfair. The tradition of the liberation struggle, which you have mentioned, entails exactly that, that all the peoples in Yugoslavia had the right to self-determination and secession. This is a very important part of our tradition. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is the most important single tradition or heritage of that struggle a unified state of all the Yugoslav peoples?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, this is an important tradition of our peoples, but let me also repeat this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No need to. I've already heard that answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why are you asking, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: With the emergence of the multiparty system in the SFRY in the same period of time, 1990 and 1991, the iconography employed by the propaganda of the leading political party in Croatia, immediately before the outbreak of the war in 1991, were there any references to Croatia in its Austro-Hungarian borders? Was there any reference to Boka as always having belonged to Croatia and ready to return to the Croatian fold?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were stories and references like that, but on the opposing side, you had Serbia as having borders near Virovitica, near the White Krajina, both sides unofficially and in certain media put forward position that is were damaging for Yugoslavia as a unified state. This goes for both Serbs and Croats. Let me just remind you that Serb politicians then adored Ducic [phoen], who believed that Serbia should stretch as far as the White Krajina, or as far as Slovenia. Therefore, let's not go any further into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: These formulas used by propaganda, did this elicit any reaction in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only in Montenegro, but rather all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please try to keep to the question and not stray from the question. I'm asking you about Croatian propaganda as addressed to Montenegro. I'm asking you about reactions in Montenegro. Please try to narrow your answer down to the specific target of my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my propaganda you mean the claim that Boka Kotorska and the Montenegrin coast should belong to Croatia, I only heard Sime Djodan say anything like this, a Croatian politician. He wrote about this, and President Tudjman had him removed. But I never heard anything like this being said by anyone else, or by the Croatian press at the time, for that matter. Sime Djodan was the only exception to this. This was used both in Montenegro and in Croatia for propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just briefly: In relation to this kind of propaganda, were there negative reactions in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The people refused to come to terms with these positions, and they refused to come to terms with the fact that Boka Kotorska might belong to Croatia. But we are only talking about Sime Djodan, this one specific politician now. I did not hear anyone else make any such claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you talked about the government session held, purportedly, on the 1st of October, 1991, you said that you went to that meeting, or rather, that you came to the meeting around 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can't say if it was 8.00 or 9.00 o'clock, but night had fallen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were informed about this by police officers who had pulled you over on your way back home to Kotor. Can you tell us, please, specifically, which police officers, where, and how they informed you about this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on my way back from the airport. We were driving. My driver was there too. The Morica [phoen] Bridge, it's a roundabout route. The police officer pulled us over, and he asked me: "Minister, where are you headed for." He said: "You can't go home now because there's a government session underway and you're wanted there. Your presence is required. They want you in Podgorica." So that was our entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the car in which you drove? Was that an official car?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jugooceanija's official car. It's a Peugeot, a new one, owned by Jugooceanija. The driver's name was Zlatko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was this car marked in any special way, rotating lights, blue or red lights, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was marked or not. It was an official Jugooceanija car, the manager's car. It was evening by the time he pulled us over. We turned around. We took a different road that took us straight to the government headquarters, and I was on my way within minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen to you, before or after that police officer handed you a summons, to attend a government meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything like that happening before or after. Something similar may have happened, it's just that I can't remember now. However, it was the case in this particular instance. I did mention that I had seen off Mr. Wejnaendts on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's not go back to that now, please. You said that when you came to the government session, when you arrived there, among other people, you saw that there were generals wearing ceremonial uniforms. Can you explain this, ceremonial uniforms? What exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are uniforms they use for military drills when they go to war. It's not the same uniform that a general would wear walking about town, wearing trousers and shoes, tightened by belts, wearing caps. You can tell that it's a different kind of uniform from the one they use normally or regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me again which military officials, military officials familiar to you, were present at the government meeting held on the 1st of October, 1991, as you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar was present, General Jeremic. Let me tell you, however: I didn't know these people personally except that they were pointed out to me. Babic was there, who was a member of the cabinet, General Damjanovic, and other military officers whom I did not know. They were seated in the row behind them. There was a group of officers attending the meeting who had never been cabinet members or anything. The atmosphere was tense. The lighting was quite dim. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: General Strugar, General Damjanovic, General Babic, and who else?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Jeremic, because that's what they said his name was. I didn't personally know them. I saw them right there for the first time, with the exception of General Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You say General Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what his name was. I'm not sure, however. Please don't make me go there, because I said before that I didn't know those people. They just told me what their names were. I think it was Jeremic. And there were some other colonels there, I believe, who were seated in the row behind the generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can I please just complete my question before you answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said was Admiral Jokic there. What else should my answer be?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please stop interrupting me and allow me to finish my sentence. Admiral Jokic, was he present at the meeting on the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic was not present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this a categorical statement on your part?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you remember clearly now that he did not attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember clearly. I may have made a mistake when --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please. May I just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a police interrogation. You're an attorney at law. I can provide whatever answers I like to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In connection with General Jeremic, could this possibly have been General Jeremija?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that may well be the case. I didn't know the people. I was just told what their names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: About these military officials, generals, what were their positions, their specific positions at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not entirely. I know that General Strugar was said to have been the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, and that prior to that, if no longer at that point, he was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Montenegro. General Strugar was the most important person in the group. You could tell by the way they were seated and by the way he was treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who told you this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A neighbour of mine, the one that I was seated next to. The meeting was quite far along. It was night. And I asked him who the people were and he told me and I saw the way those people were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this neighbour who told you that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is one of the ministers sitting next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: By the name of?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markovic, if I remember correctly. He was the justice secretary. I forgot his first name. He was sitting next to me. He was the justice minister. And he told me who the people were. I think Abramovic, the agriculture minister, also told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you said Markovic --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Markovic, yes. I'm not sure if that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let us avoid confusion, because you're referring to the Ministry of Justice. I believe the minister was Momcilo Knezevic at the time.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that after?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was then. It was then. I think it was Knezevic. And he was also in the same place. Now, I don't know. I can't tell. Knezevic was seated just opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. About the remaining three generals, Jeremija, Damjanovic, and Babic of whom you said that he was the Defence minister, Jeremija and Damjanovic. Do you know what their respective positions were at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I was never told, and I didn't think about it. They were just there. And they didn't speak much at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you asked about Strugar, did you perhaps ask anyone who the other generals were, Jeremija and Damjanovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In terms of their position. I mean what they did.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. In your statement of 2000, on page 10, I will read to you what you said. I also noticed the fact that about ten highly positioned JNA officials were there, all wearing camouflage combat uniforms. The only ones that I recognised were General Pavle Strugar, commander of the JNA units attacking Dubrovnik, General Radomir Jeremija, the commander of the Uzice Corps, Radomir Damjanovic, commander of the Podgorica Corps; Admiral Miodrag Jokic, soon to become the commander of the Boka Kotorska military naval sector; and Bozo Babic, the Minister of Defence for Montenegro. That was your statement back in 2000 to the investigators of the Tribunal, whereas the answer you have provided today is quite different and there's quite a large discrepancy between your answer today and the statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the discrepancy. What is the discrepancy you're talking about? I'm afraid I don't understand. What exactly do you mean? Well, explain, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just take it easy, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I take a moment just to firstly object to the fact that Mr. Rodic is not making reference to the document provided by the OTP before the testimony arose as to corrections to the statement provided by the witness to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague Somers is right. Before the examination-in-chief, I received from her this document, without any signature and any specific mark. And I trust that this document was drawn up by her, but the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal say very clearly how corrections to the statements are to be made, and that is in the same way in which the statements are taken. We have had numerous examples of subsequent amendments and changes; however, here I don't see either the signature of Mr. Samardzic or any specific remarks that this is a corrected version. So if my colleague would like to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will indeed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That is for 92 bis, where the witness is not coming live to give direct testimony. When the statement is either affirmed in the field by members of the Registry or a local notarial type of official, and there are corrections to be made. And that is the reference to the format in which it is done. Live testimony can always be corrected when there is an observation by the witness that there is something wrong. This is not a 92 bis witness; far from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I ask, Ms. Somers: Are you saying that the corrections are ones that were made just before the witness came to give evidence, or are they corrections that were made at the time of the original statement in 2000? I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, sir. These are not from 2000. These were made -- an investigator, upon being informed that there were several corrections to be made -- this is to a very lengthy statement given in a language other than the native tongue of Mr. Samardzic, in -- under circumstances that were indicated to us were very difficult, following, I understand, a bout of bad health, and a lengthy read-back in a language not his own, he pointed out certain things that he thought needed to be corrected. We got what we were told by way of having an investigator speak to him, and presented these to the Defence so that they would have ample opportunity to inquire on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I think we can accept that there was a statement in 2000, and you have correctly put the relevant parts of that to the witness. We are told that the two sheets of paper you have are corrections made when the witness came to give evidence here, and I think you can frame any further questions you want in that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. And regarding the corrections, I would also like to note that I have an official and certified statement made by this witness, and I would like just to draw to your attention that our next witness, Djelo Jusic, also made an official and verified statement, and also, after this statement, he provided officially signed and authenticated changes to his statement. However, this one I received only minutes before the witness entered this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that all you're putting at the moment, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to add, specifically regarding this issue: In the 2000 statement, what my question referred to was repeated seven times, and I think that this fully justifies my posing this question and raising this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no question about that, Mr. Rodic, and you have, I believe, put the 2000 form, identifying who was present, to the witness, and that is clear on the record and clear in our minds. The concern of Ms. Somers is that you, in your questioning, gave no acknowledgment to the fact that there has been a correction indicated by the witness which today would change the identity of some of the people that he can recall being at the meeting. That's the substance of the matter. The technicality of this debate concerns whether or not there has -- you should have been provided with a signed and properly authenticated statement of corrections. I haven't turned back to the Rules, but in regard to that, I believe Ms. Somers may be correct when she says that the strict requirement of the Rules is that of Rule 92 bis rather than the situation we're now dealing with. It does occur to me, though, Ms. Somers, that to be simply given a sheet of paper with no signature on it is a measure of informality which could lead to a level of dissatisfaction. If there are significant changes to a statement, the changes ought at least to be signed and dated, if that's going to be the basis of notification of changes to the other party, just as a matter of practicality and authentication.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would in no way quarrel with the Chamber's position because of the circumstances, we wanted to make sure that the Defence had adequate notice and that they were not prejudiced. I do want to comment about Mr. Jusic's correction. It is, if the Defence takes notes, from a 92 bis interview in the field, in connection with, if I'm correct, another case, and the statement is being -- and I believe the case most likely would have been Milosevic. I can check, but I recall very definitely seeing the 92 bis certifications in connection therewith. So there is a difference, and of course they do have those particular prior statements under 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Rodic, we've spent enough time debating both the substance and the technical requirements. I think we all know where we stand, and certainly in 2000, one list of people present was given, a different list is now the subject of the evidence, and you've correctly drawn attention to those changes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By accepting this suggestion of yours, I would now like to ask a question of the witness, based on this just-received correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And my question is: How could it be possible that just prior to the trial of Mr. Strugar, how could he possibly remember now that General Jokic was not present at the meeting he mentioned? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory was not refreshed now. I immediately remember that. And when I testified in the Milosevic case, I also said that Jokic was not there. I noticed the mistake. I don't know if I'm to blame or the people who were in Sydney with me. I was just discharged from the hospital at the time. It was just an oversight on my part. I don't remember if I mentioned his name or not. But as soon as I noticed this error, I reacted, and when I testified the last time before the Court, I said that Jokic was not there, and I don't want to claim that, because he wasn't. It was just an error that occurred and that I believe was corrected not today, but more than a year ago, when I testified against Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I think that you were not so adamant when you testified at the Milosevic's case concerning the presence of General Jokic. However, I will keep this reservation, and after our next break, I intend to check the records and the transcripts to see whether I was wrong or -- whether I was right or not. You made your statement in the year 2000, given to the investigators. You said that you read this statement and signed it. You yourself stated that you speak several languages, particularly English, that you were a foreign minister, in which position I presume that most frequently you used English in your diplomatic contact. And for a long time now you have been living in Australia, where, as far as I know, English is also spoken there. Therefore, the B/C/S version of your statement, which is your mother tongue, and the 2000 statement made in English, should not be of any problem for you when reading them. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the statement made in 2000 happened only two or three or four days after my discharge from the hospital, when I lost my legs. So it was only to be expected for me to make more errors than under normal circumstances. In addition to that, I don't think that these are major mistakes, and I really made an effort to rectify them subsequently. I know, as a lawyer, you insist on them, but it was no bad intention on my side to give misinformation. Because even back then, in the year 2000, I was too unwell and my health was so bad to enable me to remember what exactly happened nine years before. So there was no ill intention on my part, and there were other minor mistakes that I also rectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. And also without any ill intention -- ill intent on my part, I would like draw your attention now to what you stated in 2000, and the volume and the way it was represented, and just focussing on one fact proves that I was right. So on page 10, you said: "The only ones that I recognised," which means that you didn't ask anyone - you say: "I recognised were the generals Pavle Strugar, Jeremija, Radomir Damjanovic, Miodrag Jokic, and Bozo Babic." Further on, on page -- on the next page, paragraph 2, where you mention that General Strugar said that he was happy that the Montenegrins were going to fight, he said that his words were echoed by Jeremija, Damjanovic, Jokic, and particularly by Babic, who spoke a lot. So you even mention here that Jokic took floor at this meeting. Also, on the same page, the next paragraph, where you describe -- where you mention Kristo Djurovic, in your last sentence in the B/C/S version, you said: "Instead, Jokic attended the meeting, and he was fully in support of the attack, and who was later to become Djurovic's successor." Then on the next page, in paragraph 1, you say: "Based on my knowledge, I cannot say what actually happened, but I can say that within an hour, Jokic was prepared to take his command duty, and that is after Djurovic had been killed." On page 19, paragraph 3 from the top, you say: "During this period, I had an opportunity to talk to Strugar and Jokic. That was the only contact that I had with them after the 1st of October meeting, which implies that Jokic was there on the 1st of October." And also on this same page, paragraph 4, you said -- when you called Strugar and Jokic regarding the British men, you say that there was no insolence that they demonstrated at the meeting of the 1st of October, and before that you said that someone had provided telephone numbers of Strugar and Jokic. I believe that you have stated seven times, quite decidedly, not only of the presence of Jokic at the meeting, but also that he spoke at the meeting, and that you even communicated during the meeting on the 1st of October. So it cannot be seen as an error, a minor error, or any other error that you would like to represent here today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. My conversation with Jokic was on the phone, and it happened much later after the 1st of October. It was sometime in November. And this conversation has nothing to do with the 1st of October. Further -- allow me to continue. So that was the first mistake which was perpetuated, and I didn't react to that in time, so it just remained in the text. But as soon as I noticed this, I reacted. At first, I did not notice this oversight. It was just an error. Because there was no reason for me to say that Jokic was there if he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But what reason could you have to say that his words were echoed by Strugar and Jokic? Who imputed that to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever did that, it wasn't Jokic who could have echoed that, because he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why did you say that six times in the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not six times. You are talking rubbish. It says that once it was Jokic who echoed. One mistake was made when the name of Jokic was inserted, and it was perpetuated. I explained that during my testimony at the Milosevic case as soon as I noticed that that was a mistake. And I think that that was not even my mistake, but the people who wrote down my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I read to you passages from your statement where you have repeatedly mentioned, seven times, that General Jokic was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if you say that it's been repeated 70 times, Jokic was not there. It just somehow slipped in. Because there are 34 pages of this statement, so it's quite to be expected that these kind of errors could occur, especially if the statement was given by a man who was very ill, who was just discharged from the hospital. And even if I said so - and I don't think I did - because at first I couldn't remember all the names. There were five or six people with me in Sydney. They were just asking me: Was this person there, was that person there? I confirmed, and that is how this happened. However, my conversation that I had in late October or early November with Jokic has nothing to do with the 1st of October meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We shall come later to that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the one who raised these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that later. After you were discharged from the hospital, did anyone coerce you into making a statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no coercion. I gave it on my own free will. But I can't say that I was perfectly healthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did any of the investigators insert seven incorrect statements in your statement that you after that signed, after you have read it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't phrase it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Phrase it in your own way.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that there was a mistake while I spoke with Mr. Williamson, who speaks in a Louisiana accent, different from my Australia accent, and it is obvious that certain mistakes occurred. In addition, the translation into the B/C/S is not compatible and not adequate to the one that I made in English. So if we analyse both, we could discover many, many more mistakes. There are some wrong dates and things like that which were beyond my control. For instance, I just recently looked at it, and it says that the Lord Carrington's project was discussed on the 6th of October, instead of it was on the 7th of October. And there are many more things like that. About if you wish to use that against him, you are free to do that. The translation is very bad. You cannot translate folklore poems into English, giving them a totally different meaning, and then impute that to me. Please, we can hardly reach any truth if we work on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You are fully -- you're completely right, and I agree with you. But I am not talking about wrong dates, about the Louisiana accent, wrong figures and dates. The issue here is a person, large enough and important enough, for whom, among other things, it is said here on seven occasions that he was present there and that he even took the floor. I wouldn't compare this with the wrong translation or anything like that, and I really don't see how can anyone erroneously translate from English into B/C/S that Jokic was present at the meeting, because that is also the B/C/S version says, the translation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of this is correct. I've only given you several examples. I must repeat this again: There was an error, with no ill intent, which I corrected in time. Now you can say whatever you like, but there was no ill will, no bad intentions behind it. The first time I realised there was an error when I testified in the Milosevic case over a year ago, I said clearly that Jokic wasn't there. I think that should be sufficient explanation, both for yourself, Mr. Rodic, and for the Tribunal itself. No one forced me to say that Jokic was there. When I testified in the Milosevic case, I said immediately that Jokic wasn't there. There is absolutely no intent, no intention on my part to place Jokic there. You can criticise me, you can judge me, because I did make an error, but there was no ill intent behind this error, and this error has been set right. I don't think it's an essential error, anyway, no matter how much you insist on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Samardzic. And now for what I've promised. In your testimony in the Milosevic case, on page 11185, lines 21 and 22, you say that "present at the meeting there were military officials, three or four generals wearing combat uniform." You never made any reference to him as not being there, nor did you make any corrections in relation to your statement of 2000. And along the same lines, let me just say this: If you don't trust me, if you don't believe that what I've read out to you is true, if you don't believe that there are seven references in your statement to Admiral Jokic being there, do you wish to have the English statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. What is being presented is not the complete version of the testimony, to the best of my recollection, and we'd ask to be given an opportunity, if this is going to persist, to have the actual question and the actual answer about who was present, from the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could there be an accurate reading of the relevant questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try, if you allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're talking about page 11185, and there's a reference in line 13, the following reference: [In English], "Was then a meeting was held, the extraordinary session, or rather, expanded, enlarged session, as it was referred to?" [Interpretation] That's part of the previous answer. The question: [In English] "What was discussed?" [Interpretation] Answer: [In English] "I came to the meeting late. I wasn't there from the beginning, but towards the end, because President Bulatovic sent me, with Lord Carrington's deputy, Mr. Wejnaendts, to visit Cetinje. So when I went into the hall, I was quite shocked. I have never seen a meeting of that kind. There were about eight military persons, three or four generals, at least, wearing war uniforms, and they were sitting at the tables that we would usually sit at when we held government meetings, and the entire leadership of Montenegro was there, who were not government members led by President Bulatovic." [Interpretation] Next question, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I will endeavour during redirect to give you the complete line of questioning on this matter from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we have that much into the transcript. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I think, if you wish to pursue the question of what was said at the Milosevic trial, it would probably be useful for you for that to be done when we next resume, so that you've had an opportunity to consider it in full, unless you're about to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I have not quite understood what you're saying. Do you mean that we should have a break now and run a check on this, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. I understand now. My error. I apologise. I will then continue discussing this later on and continue my examination on this particular issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, during the examination-in-chief by the OTP, in answer to questions about who said what at that meeting, a meeting held on the 1st of October, you said a number of times that General Strugar had said that Montenegro had been attacked by 30.000 Ustashe. You state that he said this a number of times, that he said that we had been attacked and that we had to defend ourselves, that 30.000 Ustashe were encroaching on Montenegro. He said that we would defend Yugoslavia with minimum losses, and so on and so forth. So you say this at least two or three times in the course of your examination-in-chief, about General Strugar saying this and about that being the first thing you heard, having joined the meeting. And then you go on to say that Momir Bulatovic, the president of Montenegro's presidency, and other people there, said the same thing later on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is perfectly correct, but you're trying to twist my words around. General Strugar said that 30.000 Ustashe were encroaching on Boka and that we had to defend ourselves. The first thing [As interpreted] you said was that we have been attacked. There are 30.000 Ustashe and we have to defend ourselves. Momir Bulatovic repeated the same thing, and other speakers also said that we should defend ourselves. I said it too. I said if we were attacked, well, then, we should defend ourselves. I see no particular distinction there, and nothing contentious. It is now 12 years later that I'm trying to memorise the exact words spoken on that occasion, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Again, I must ask you: Do you still stand by your statement, what you said now about the information on 30.000 Ustashe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is a misquotation of the record. What was said on the unofficial record that I have from the -- it appears on page 26, line 11: "Was that the first you heard of these 30.000 Ustashe suggestion," not the first thing you heard. So if perhaps we could just make sure that that is what was -- the thrust of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, there may be a distinction there, Mr. Rodic, but I don't think it's critical to your questioning. So if you want to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. I will then phrase my question differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where was it that you first heard that an attack on Cena Gora [phoen] was in the offing, or rather that 30.000 Ustashe were about to attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard this was from General Strugar and Momir Bulatovic. They were sitting next to one another, or rather they occupied the other sides of the table but they were saying the same thing, that we had been attacked, that 30.000 Ustashe were encroaching on Montenegro, were invading Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. The essence of my question is not about distinction between attack and encroach. But what I want to know is whether General Strugar and Mr. Bulatovic spoke at the same time. What I want to know is who was the first to say this? Who was the first person you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Strugar. However, according to my information, Momir Bulatovic said the same thing. Maybe he even said it earlier than Strugar, or maybe even before I arrived. I don't know what they had been talking about at the meeting before I arrived, before I entered the conference room. However, when I came in, General Strugar was the one who said 30.000 Ustashe are on their way and we have to defend ourselves. And then Bulatovic spoke and some other ministers spoke. So the sequence itself, I can't remember who spoke directly after Bulatovic spoke. Knezevic, Abramovic, they all spoke later. Even Obradovic, who opposed the war, spoke. I think he was the education minister. And that was the general course of the debate, and that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you look at it logically, you said that this was a government meeting, an expanded session. And if you look at the logic of the situation, who should be expected to be the first to speak at such a meeting? You being a member of the cabinet, so you should know who opens the meeting and who speaks first.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was practically the introduction of military administration in Montenegro. This was no ordinary session of the cabinet. During usual sessions, half the seats are empty, and this evening, the room was full. It was crammed with ministers, generals, assistant ministers, military people. It was a session behind closed doors, and this was the introduction of military administration, to all practical intents and purposes, in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
