utterances.text: So let me get this clear. This was no ordinary government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, please understand. I'm not interested in what sort of a session, meeting it was. My question is trying to focus on the essence of this matter. In view of who was present, the cabinet, okay, the expanded cabinet. So we may have visitors, for example, the president of the Presidency of Montenegro and military officials and generals. In view of the presence of the ministers, the Prime Minister, the president of the state, and the generals there, is there an inherent logic to the situation? Who would have been the first to speak? Who was the most senior person present?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency. However, he did not preside over the session. So according to the same logic, it might as well have been General Strugar to speak first, because there was a war in the offing. A war was about to begin. So there's another logic there you could apply. However, neither of them were presiding over the meeting. They were the two key figures at the meeting, although they were not technically presiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. General Strugar was the first person to say this, and he was the first person you heard this from. And then after that, Momir Bulatovic echoed his words?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't rule out the possibility that Momir Bulatovic said this before I got there. I can't rule that out. I'm only telling you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I want to hear about. That's precisely what I want to know. You heard General Strugar say this. He was the first person you heard. But Momir Bulatovic may have said it before you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's because the meeting had already been in course for two hours before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On page 10 of your statement, dated 2002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you're coming in much too quickly for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On page 10 of your statement of 2000, the statement you gave to the investigators, in the last paragraph, you state the following: "Djukanovic presided over the meeting but Bulatovic was present too. Bulatovic spoke about 30.000 Ustashe attacking Montenegro and that we had to defend ourselves." The first person you refer to in your statement in connection with this 30.000 Ustashe claim is Bulatovic. And let me tell you something else too. Before the end of your 34-page statement, you make several references to the specific number, 30.000 Ustashe. But there's not a single reference in your entire statement to the name of General Strugar as being in any sort of connection with anything like this being said, this claim being made, or you ever hearing anything like that. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you want me to say. Even the first time around, I said that I heard General Strugar say this. I never said that he never said this. But this 30.000 Ustashe claim, General Strugar was not the only one to bring it up. They heard from General Strugar, all the others, that there were 30.000 Ustashe, so everyone -- this just perpetuated itself, this 30.000 figure. That's what I said and that's what you find written in my statement. I never said that General Strugar did not say this, but at the same time I must point out that other people present at the meeting, other ministers, were making references to 30.000 Ustashas, because this was something that they had heard from General Strugar and from Momir Bulatovic before I even walked in. Therefore, there is no discrepancy or contradiction whatsoever, as you're trying to insinuate. I see no contradiction there. That's precisely how it was. 30.000 Ustashe about to attack Montenegro. I took this in, because I was there, and later this turned out not to have been true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Be my guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: A while ago we had a discussion on a very simple issue before we managed to agree. Again, in the year 2000, which was the first interview you had with the investigators, and you provided a written statement, you said what I assume was the first thing you laid eyes on when you walked into the meeting: "Bulatovic spoke about 30.000 Ustashe about to attack Montenegro and that we had to defend ourselves." It is still my submission to you that in this statement, there is not a single reference by name to General Strugar as even having repeated this 30.000 Ustashe claim, unequivocally, let alone stating that he was the first person you heard this 30.000 Ustashe claim from. So my question to you now is how do you explain the discrepancy between your statement here today and as stated in your 2000 statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no difference between the two whatsoever. General Strugar said 30.000 and Momir Bulatovic also said 30.000, and this was a benchmark for the rest of us there. General Strugar was a professional. Please allow me to finish. His reputation was great, and even what Momir Bulatovic was saying, the assumption was that he must have heard it from General Strugar. Bulatovic spoke about it. Milo Djukanovic spoke about it. Other ministers who were there spoke about it. It's all about the psychology of perception, how this seeps into your head. So the assumption is that a professional military man, a general, would have been the first to say it. The reason I didn't point out General Strugar and single him out in my statement is because I simply didn't think it necessary. I don't think anyone else would have even made any reference to 30.000 Ustashe had it not been for General Strugar's presence at the meeting. That's precisely why he was there, why he came to the meeting to tell us that a army was about to attack and it was our duty to defend ourselves. That was the purpose of the whole meeting, that was the purpose of his presence at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me turn this around now. The same thing you just told us now, why didn't you say the same thing to the investigators back in 2000?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I didn't? That's precisely what I told them, that General Strugar was there, that 30.000 Ustashe were about to attack Montenegro. Just ask the investigators. What you're putting to me that the first investigator spoke and the second investigator and then the next one, there was no need for us to talk at cross-purposes like that. General Strugar and all the remaining generals who were present at the meeting were there to tell us that a foreign army was about to attack Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. We've heard that already.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, the essential difference is: Why didn't you tell the investigators back in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, I didn't? Of course I did. Maybe not in the same sequence that you're giving us now. Please allow me. I told the investigators precisely as I remembered. I was in a state of shock that evening, and it was my deepest conviction that the army would never attack Dubrovnik, despite all your stories about Croats doing this or doing that or what was in the offing. Your stories just a while ago. Of course that's what I mean. It was my deepest conviction that the JNA would not move to attack Dubrovnik, a peaceful town, that they would not start out to demolish that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But that was not my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a statement I'm making now. What I wish to say is -- you're asking me about the things that happened that night. I was deeply shocked by what I had heard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you please caution the witness to provide brief answers to my questions. If he doesn't have an answer, then he might as well say that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know plenty. I know more than you believe I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be a profitable time for us to conclude this afternoon's session. We've gone a little over time because you were on an important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we have fully appreciated the point that you're making. Before we break, could I mention the issue of the Prosecution request for protective measures in respect of a future witness. The only issue is whether there should be facial, voice, and pseudonym measures accorded. Is there any objection to that, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to ask you to have a moment, in view of the essence of this issue. Can we please go into private session for this? We have a brief answer, but also I'm rather worried by the presence of the witness here in the courtroom. I'll try to keep my explanation down to just a couple of words, or Mr. Samardzic may as well stay, in order to save time. But can we please have private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only comment that the purpose of private session is defeated by the retained presence of the witness, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, thank you very much for your evidence today. We must ask you to return when we resume on Monday, at 9.00 in the morning. I wonder if you'd now go with the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.54 p.m.
